title: Trump breaks off Taj Mahal bondholder talks amid looming bankruptcy
description_medium: On November 13, 1990, Donald Trump ended negotiations with bondholders over restructuring the Taj Mahal casino’s debt, putting the project closer to bankruptcy. He faced a $47.3 million interest payment and bondholders sought equity and debt concessions. The dispute continued into a negotiated Chapter 11 restructuring later that week.
description_long: Donald Trump’s Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City faced a major debt crisis in November 1990. Trump had a $47.3 million interest payment due on bonds used to finance the casino and was negotiating with creditors over restructuring the debt. On November 13 he broke off talks, moving the project toward a possible Chapter 11 filing. Bondholder representative Wilbur Ross had pressed for debt concessions and a substantial ownership stake; Trump objected to the proposal. Negotiations resumed, and by November 16 Trump and bondholders had reached an agreement to put the casino through a prepackaged bankruptcy, allowing its $675 million bond issue to be restructured. The deal reduced interest costs and gave creditors a stake in the casino. The November break in talks was one moment in a broader financial dispute; it does not establish that Ross alone caused the casino’s near-bankruptcy or that Trump assigned him sole blame.

corrected_wording.proposed: Trump breaks off Taj Mahal bondholder talks amid looming bankruptcy
corrected_wording.reason: The replacement identifies the documented event and avoids the original title’s unsupported or misattributed claim.

source_access_notes: Opened the Nov. 14, 1990 Washington Post report on Trump ending bondholder talks and the UPI account of the Nov. 16 restructuring.
rationale: The Nov. 13 rupture occurred while Trump faced a $47.3 million interest payment; the subsequent restructuring shows why the talks mattered without assigning Ross sole responsibility for the casino’s financial distress.

title: Fred Trump buys $3.35 million in Trump Castle casino chips in 1990
description_medium: In December 1990, Fred Trump’s lawyer Howard Snyder bought $3.35 million in chips at Donald Trump’s Castle casino without gambling, according to New Jersey gaming records described by the Washington Post and New York Times. The transaction functioned as an interest-free loan to help Donald meet a bond payment. New Jersey regulators later imposed a civil penalty over the transaction.

Snyder exchanged it for $5,000 gambling chips and left without placing a bet, according to New Jersey gaming records reported by the Washington Post and the New York Times. Donald Trump used the funds to meet an interest payment on the casino’s debt. The New York Times described the arrangement as an illegal loan under New Jersey gaming law and reported a $65,000 civil penalty. The records show how Fred Trump supplied liquidity to his son’s casino during a period of financial strain. This transaction followed earlier family financing and differs from the 1954 FHA inquiry into Fred Trump’s apartment projects. New Jersey regulators imposed a civil penalty over the transaction, while the records described in these reports show no criminal charge against Donald Trump.
